p3_b4.ocr: The second table categorizes key clinical clues, beginning with general history, which includes delayed gross motor milestones, developmental coordination disorder, being double-jointed in sports, showing hypermobility “tricks” during childhood, giving up sports due to recurrent injuries, mild generalized muscle weakness, unexplained musculoskeletal pain, easy fatigability, and paresthesias. The medical history encompasses recurrent (sub)luxations, tendon and muscle rupture, anal prolapse in childhood, reduced effect of local anesthesia, complications of surgery, easy bruising, abnormal wound healing, uterus prolapse or cervical insufficiency, early onset varicose veins, pneumothorax or pneumohematothorax, spontaneous arterial rupture, clubfoot, intestinal or uterine fragility, severe scoliosis at birth, and congenital bilateral hip dislocation.

p3_b5.ocr: Family history notes generalized hypermobility and sudden death (vascular type). Physical examination reveals generalized joint hypermobility, increased skin hyperextensibility, smooth skin, wide atrophic scars, molluscoid pseudotumors, subcutaneous feroids, thin skin, characteristic facial appearance, gingival recessions, microcornea, and congenital kyphoscoliosis. Neurological examination indicates mild proximal weakness, mild reduction of vibration sense, and reduction of tendon reflexes. Ancillary investigations show nerve conduction studies indicating reduction of CMAP, electromyography showing a mixed pattern, normal or mildly elevated CK, normal or mildly myopathic muscle biopsy features, heart imaging revealing mitral valve prolapse or aortic dilatation, and bone computer mineralometry indicating early onset osteopenia.
